note: In-session one-vendor panel under D154(b) as amended by D155, on dataset 10.0.2 (D182). It is the 2026-11-02 run (2026-11-02T19-36-46-976Z-in_session, dataset 10.0.0) with its Anticipation and Experimentation cells and indicator audits replaced by a rerun made on 2026-11-03, because D182 changed the per-head denominators in both dimensions, which changed every brief there and dropped 260 of the 1215 cells under D160. The other seven dimensions are the 2026-11-02 run's cells as recorded, and their brief hashes match dataset 10.0.2. The rerun (2026-11-03T08-47-29-180Z-in_session, kept beside this file) used the same three panelists: institutionalist on claude-opus-5-5, bottom_up on claude-opus-5-5, wealth_sceptic on claude-sonnet-5-5, all Anthropic, through Claude Code subagents run by a Claude Code orchestrating session (Claude Opus 5.5). It covered both dimensions for all 135 countries, 270 cells, with prompts built by pnpm bench delphi --in-session --dimensions anticipation,experimentation at the current prompt version, byte-identical to a gateway run's for those two dimensions. Each panelist answered in batches of 27 countries, one fresh context per batch and per round, and the audit in one context per stance, so no context held two stances and none saw another panelist's text except the anonymised round-1 summary the round-2 prompt carries. Quality control by the orchestrator: every batch was counted for repeated rationales and for missingEvidence lists with no country-specific item, and none was found. Two round-2 batches returned 26 of 27 countries (wealth_sceptic without Haiti, institutionalist without Sri Lanka); each missing country was answered in its own fresh context on the same stance and model. Several wealth_sceptic batches skimmed the NO DATA and NOT SCORED paragraphs that repeat word for word across countries, and two wrote their answers through a script holding hand-written per-country entries. Panelists drew on their own knowledge where the system rules allow it, and those claims are unverified. No call failed. One vendor means the spread measures stance, not vendor, and shared model-family blind spots are hidden by a narrow IQR, which is a floor on real uncertainty (D155). A multi-vendor or gateway run supersedes this one. This is an interpretation layer: its estimates reach only delphiScore and delphiIqr, and blendedScore only where a dimension has no observed indicator; they never enter score.

indicatorJudgements.rationale: Registrations are the result of intention passing through the formal registry, so they are an outcome of agency and of the registry's reach together, not a direct capability measure. Formality rises with income and the count misses informal activity.

Days to register measured how fast the state's registry turns an intention into a legal entity, a sound institutional measure. Retirement is right because the series is frozen and business entry efficiency carries the construct.

It scores the institutional friction between an intention and a legal entity, which is what the state controls in agency. Adding cost lets income per head back in somewhat, and the 82-country coverage leaves gaps.

A count of required steps reads the design of the registration regime with little income content. It is frozen at 2019, so it reads rules that may since have changed, and it overlaps the entry efficiency score.

Doing a digital task in the last three months is a behaviour that depends heavily on device and connection access, which money buys. It reads digital participation more than the capacity to turn intention into action.

Felt control is an individual attitude, and it is exactly the kind of claim that can read high where institutions give people little real room to act, as Vietnam and Nicaragua show. Response style differences across cultures add noise.

Counts only intentions that become registered limited liability companies, so it systematically undercounts action in economies where most enterprise is informal, and it is better read as an outcome of formalisation than a direct capability. Formal LLC registration rises with income and with tax regime design.
Registration delay is a regulatory condition on agency, not agency itself, and only binds people who choose the formal route. Retired and superseded by business entry efficiency.

Friction of formal entry is an input condition, and the cost component scales with income so it re-imports wealth. It says nothing about the many people who act without registering, and covers only 82 of 135 countries.
A count of bureaucratic steps is a condition on formal entry, not action, and is frozen at 2019. Less income-driven than cost measures but still measures the formal gate only.

Counting a performed task is closer to action than a skill stock, but the named tasks (file attachments, spreadsheet formulas) are office-desktop tasks that miss mobile-first action such as mobile money or WhatsApp commerce common in low-income countries. Device ownership drives much of the variation.

Felt capacity to act is a perception, but it is one of the few rows that reaches people outside the formal economy, which matters for this dimension. Response style and autocratic deference distort it, yet its income gradient is weak.

Registered limited companies are an outcome of intention turning into action, but the formal register hides informal activity that dominates poorer economies, so it rises with formality and income. Registration rules and tax incentives distort it.
Registration time is a friction input, not action itself. Retired and superseded by business_entry_efficiency, so it should carry no weight.

It scores the rules and cost of entry, which is the barrier to action rather than the action. Mixes time with cost and a foreign-firm route, and B-READY covers only 82 of 135 countries with likely skew to reforming and richer states.
Counting steps is a bureaucratic friction input and not a capability to act. Less income-linked than money-based measures, but frozen at 2019 and says little about the present.

Doing digital tasks follows device and connectivity access, which is purchased, and digital tasks are only a thin slice of turning intention into action. Self-reported, with coverage that drops most of the poorer frame.
It captures felt capacity to act, which is adjacent to agency but not action. Response style differs by culture and autocracies read high, though the income link is moderate and not dominant.

The construct, the state's capacity to implement policy, is central to coordination, but the WGI measures expert and firm opinion and tracks log income at 0.91. Retirement is right until delivery records replace it.
The same WGI perception under another name, with a construct tilted to market-friendly regulation rather than coordination. Retirement is right.
Freight forwarders' views of a country read trade scale and private logistics as much as public agencies acting together. Retirement is right.

Border time was a concrete reading of customs, standards and port agencies working together on one shipment. Retirement is right because the series is frozen and trade compliance efficiency carries it.

Border compliance is one of the few places where several agencies must act as one system, so it observes inter-agency coordination directly. It is narrow, the switch to firm reports adds perception, and cost terms carry some income.

Spending that matches the approved budget shows that the legislature, finance ministry and line agencies hold to one plan, which is coordination through formal institutions. A rigid budget that ignores a shock reads well too, so it rewards discipline over responsiveness.
The source is an executive opinion survey, so it is a perception, not a direct measure, and its microdata is not inspectable. Exclusion is right.

Autonomous, dense civil society organisations are durable vehicles for independent actors to organise, so the construct fits. It is expert-coded and closely tied to liberal democracy, so it should be filed as a perception, and it reads freedom to organise more than effective organising.
Joint public-private delivery is a strong institutional test of coordination if measured as delivered programmes rather than finance volumes. With no definition and no data, the score is provisional.
An expert and firm perception composite that correlates 0.91 with log income, and it reads state delivery rather than actors organising among themselves. Retirement is right.
Same WGI perception of wealth under a different name, and regulation quality is a condition on coordination, not coordination. Retirement is right.
International forwarders' view of a country captures only formal export logistics and penalises small or informal trade systems. Retirement is right.
Border time is an outcome of agencies acting together but on one formal channel only, and informal cross-border trade, large in Africa and South Asia, is invisible. Retired and superseded.

An outcome of formal border agencies cooperating, with a cost term that tracks income; it reads state customs performance, not whether independent actors can organise. Informal cross-border trade networks, which are a real coordination capability, are excluded.

An observable, not perception-based, read of plan-to-action alignment inside government with a modest income gradient. It is intra-state execution rather than coordination among independent actors, so it sits closer to Building.
The underlying item is a WEF executive opinion survey, so it is a perception, not a C; I refile it as P. It also sees only a formal, research-intensive slice of coordination.

Closest row to independent actors organising, and V-Dem coders do see informal and grassroots associations, but it is expert-coded, so I file it as P. It reads political openness as much as organising capacity, and its income gradient is moderate.
The right construct only if it counts joint delivery including community and cooperative partners, not only formal PPP contracts, which would track finance depth and income. No data.
A perception composite correlated 0.91 with log GDP per head, so it mostly reports national wealth. Retirement is correct.
Same expert and firm opinion as government effectiveness under another name; counts the same wealth perception twice. Retirement is correct.
A freight forwarder survey of how a country looks to global firms, shaped by port size and income. Retired rightly.

Border time is an observable result of agencies acting together, so it is an outcome rather than a capability measure. Hours fall with customs automation that wealthier states can buy; retired and superseded.

Firm-reported time and cost at the border, a delivered result of several agencies, so O. It bundles cost, imports and online ordering, picks up income-linked infrastructure and covers only 82 of 135 countries.

Spending close to the approved plan is a recorded act of coordinating ministries around an objective, and poor countries can do well on it. It can be gamed by padding budgets and says nothing on plan quality; coverage is uneven in dates.
The underlying item is an executive opinion survey, so it is P and not C. Opinion of collaboration tracks the size of the innovation system and income; no data, correctly excluded.
Expert-coded, so it is P and not C. It reads democratic openness more than ability to organise around shared goals, which makes it a regime-type proxy that correlates with income.

Joint delivery of national objectives would be a direct measure of organising across actors, if observed from project records. No dataset exists, and PPP finance data would just track infrastructure budgets.

Rule of law is the institutional base that lets strangers cooperate, so the construct is right, but the WGI is an opinion composite tied to income. Retirement is right; court records are the replacement.
A reputation for corruption is not corruption, and the composite tracks income closely. Retirement is right.
The time for a court to enforce a contract is how long a stranger's promise takes to become reliable, a direct institutional measure. Retirement is right because the series is frozen.
Courts that resolve commercial disputes reliably and cheaply are the formal mechanism that lets cooperation reach beyond personal networks. Cost terms and partial coverage are the weaknesses.
A reported experience of being asked for a bribe shows whether public rules hold for a stranger, a good outcome of institutional integrity. Reticence in surveys and its link to income both weaken it.

A state that obeys rulings it loses makes the rules credible to everyone, which is the institutional foundation of trust among strangers. It is expert-coded, close to the democracy index, and reads high where courts rarely rule against the state.
Homicide reads organised crime and income more than cooperation beyond the in-group. Retirement is right.

Generalised trust is the standard attitude item for the construct, but respondents can fill most people with their own circle, and it is an attitude rather than cooperation in practice. It correlates with income and with Nordic institutions.
Confidence in institutions matters for cooperation through them, but the battery rewards deference in autocracies. Leaving it unscored is right until an item separates confidence from deference.
Naming the stranger targets exactly the radius of trust this dimension asks about. It is still an attitude, and question-format differences between EVS and WVS add noise.

Clearance rate observes whether courts finish their caseload, a direct reading of the institution strangers rely on, and filing it as C is more accurate than O. A court can clear cases by dismissing them, so it should be read beside compliance and dispute measures.
A WGI perception composite that is largely an expert view of income. Retirement is right.
Reputation for corruption, near-identical to rule of law and close to income. Retirement is right.

Court speed is an institutional condition that makes stranger cooperation safer, not trust itself, and most low-income trade with strangers relies on reputation networks rather than courts. Retired and superseded.

A formal court-throughput score is an input that enables trust beyond networks, not observed cooperation, so I refile it as I. Its cost term follows income and it ignores informal enforcement such as market associations and community arbitration.

Experienced bribery at the state counter is an outcome of whether impersonal rules hold, and is better than reputation. It samples only formal registered firms, so informal operators who meet the state through other channels are not seen.
Whether the state obeys rulings is a precondition for impersonal trust but mostly reads democracy (r 0.88), and it is expert-coded. It says little about cooperation among ordinary strangers.
Homicide reads organised crime and income, not cooperation beyond the in-group; the diagnostic showed it carried mostly wealth. Retirement is right.

The standard attitudinal read, and it reaches informal populations that registry measures miss. Respondents can fill most people with their own circle, and it has a substantial income gradient driven by the Nordic cluster.
Confidence in government and courts reads deference in autocracies as much as trust, and trust in the state is not cooperation among strangers. Leaving it unscored is right.
Names the stranger directly, so it is the closest row to the construct and it reaches people outside formal institutions. Still a stated attitude, not observed cooperation.
An observable read of court throughput, but courts are a formal channel few people in large low-income countries use, so it reads judicial administration rather than stranger cooperation. No data.
A perception composite correlated 0.83 with log GDP and above 0.95 with corruption control, so it is largely reputation of wealth. Retirement is correct.
It measures reputation for corruption and follows income closely. Retired rightly.
Time to enforce is a court throughput outcome and not trust itself. Retired and replaced by dispute_resolution_efficiency, so should carry no weight.
Court throughput on commercial cases is an outcome that supports stranger cooperation; cost and process reliability make it follow state budgets. B-READY covers only 82 of 135 countries.
Experience of being asked for a bribe is behaviour, not reputation, and reads whether rules hold with strangers. Reticence biases it, and it still falls with income, but less than WGI composites.

A government obeying rulings it loses is a real test of whether rules bind the strong, though expert-coded and tied to democracy at 0.88. It does not cleanly follow income, but it mostly separates regime types.
Driven by organised crime and not by stranger cooperation; D44 showed it was the largest wealth contributor. Retirement is correct.

The standard generalised trust item, a perception proxy that is the closest thing to the construct. It correlates with income and institutions but with real exceptions, and respondents may fill 'most people' with their own circle.
Confidence in institutions is deference in autocracies and adjacent to trust beyond personal networks, not the same thing. No comparable data, and the proposed substitute reads regime type.
It names the stranger, which fits the dimension better than the general item. Still a self-report, and it should correlate strongly with interpersonal_trust outside a few cases like China.

Counted from records and not opinion, but a clearance rate says whether courts keep pace, not whether strangers trust them. No single publisher reaches the frame and it would cover rich members first.

The HCI blends child survival, health and learning-adjusted schooling, so it is an outcome of the education and health systems, not a direct capability measure. It tracks income very closely, and its last full round is 2020.
Formal training in firms is organisations building knowledge into their workforce, which is institutional learning. Coverage that skips most high-income countries makes the frame uneven.

Participation in education after school reads whether the system updates knowledge across working life, close to the construct. Coverage limited to OECD and EU members makes it unusable for the frame.

Citation share reads whether the research system produces knowledge others use, a quality outcome of research institutions. Whole counting lifts small countries through foreign co-authors, so part of the signal belongs to other systems.

A stock of schooling and survival outcomes that tracks income very closely, so I refile it as O rather than C. It counts formal schooling only and misses apprenticeships and peer learning, and it does not read how a country updates knowledge.

Observed workplace learning with a mild income gradient, and Enterprise Survey coverage favours middle-income countries. It counts only formal training in registered firms and misses on-the-job and informal apprenticeship learning, which is the dominant mode in informal economies.
Continuous adult learning is close to the construct, and including non-formal learning helps. Data exists only for rich economies, so any fill would be income-shaped.

Reads how much the world uses a country's formal research, a narrow elite slice of knowledge acquisition, and whole counting rewards co-authorship with rich systems. Field normalisation reduces the income tilt compared with raw volume.

It combines child survival, stunting and schooling, which are outcomes of income and past spending, and it measures a child's cohort, not how the country updates knowledge. Correct to O and near wealth proxy; 2020 vintage.
Firms training staff is an observed behaviour of knowledge update, and it varies a lot among middle-income countries. Coverage skips most rich states and formal-firm bias is strong.
It matches continuous learning well, but available data covers only Europe and the OECD, so a score would sort mainly by region and income. No data for the wider frame.
Quality-adjusted research output is an outcome of funding and international co-authorship, so it follows income and research-system size. Whole counting inflates small countries with big partners.

A level of unemployment reads labour market structure, informality and the business cycle more than the capacity to respond to change. It is a blunt outcome, and low values in informal economies hide underemployment.
Long spells show whether labour market institutions move people back into work, a closer reading of reallocation than the rate. Its meaning flips in tight markets, so it needs the rate beside it.
Basket concentration is a stock of product mix, an outcome rather than a direct measure of switching capacity, and it misreads high-value concentrated exporters. It should be filed as O, not C.

Entry into new export lines observes reallocation of capital and labour, which is adaptation by the economy. The fifteen-year window is slow and resource finds count as entry, so it reads structural change more than response to shocks.

Emergency agencies that prepare for and recover from shocks are the clearest institutional form of adaptability. Existing sources mix self-assessment, perception and wealth stocks, so leaving it a gap is right.

Timestamps of rule and programme changes after a new condition would observe the state adapting directly, the best measure for this dimension. It must reward fit change, not churn, which would also read as speed.

In low-income countries people cannot afford unemployment and absorb shocks through informal work, so low unemployment reads poverty and informality as much as fluid reallocation. A blunt outcome with an ambiguous sign.
Closer to slow reallocation than the headline rate, but its meaning flips in tight markets. Labour force surveys miss moves into informal work, which is the main adaptive channel in large LMICs.
A static product mix is an outcome and a structural condition, not the capacity to switch, so I refile it as O. Merchandise-only and blind to informal and domestic reallocation.
Observed reallocation into new lines, and the rate design keeps it from rewarding already-broad rich baskets. It sees only formal recorded merchandise exports and moves slowly.

Demonstrated recovery from real shocks is the right construct, and community-led response is often the main capacity in poorer countries. Every candidate source rewards stocks money buys and government self-reports. No data.
Rule-change speed is a direct read of formal system adaptation, though it misses how households and informal markets adapt without new rules. No data.
Low unemployment can mean a rigid or informal market. Poor countries often read low because few can afford to be unemployed, and the modelled estimates are partly imputed.
A high share can show slow reallocation, but a tight market also yields a high share. It needs a labour force survey, which rich countries run more, and it is ambiguous when read alone.
A basket concentration index reads product mix and resource endowment, not the ability to switch. Commodity exporters read badly and rich specialised exporters read badly for non-fragility reasons.

Entry into new export lines is observed reallocation, and the room-to-enter denominator limits the rich-country advantage. Goods only, a slow 15-year window, and catch-up countries have more room to enter.
Observed recovery from real shocks would be a direct test of response, but available sources are self-assessments and stocks that money buys. No data.
Speed of rule change is a direct response measure that wealth does not give. It could reward unstable rule-making, and no dataset exists.

Manufacturing share reads the sector structure of the economy, not the capacity to turn plans into working systems. It penalises service economies and rewards resource or assembly economies by accident.
The share reads where global value chains place assembly, so it often measures foreign firms' build capacity on domestic soil. It is an outcome only weakly tied to national building.
A freight-forwarder rating of infrastructure stock reads accumulated spending and perception, not delivery capacity. Retirement is right.
The wait for a grid connection observed a utility and permit system delivering a working connection. Retirement is right because the series is frozen.

Connection time observes state and utility delivery at small scale, but reliability of supply is largely an infrastructure stock that income buys. It reads routine service delivery, not building new systems.
Export basket sophistication is an accumulated outcome of productive capabilities and correlates strongly with income. It reads what was built, not current capacity to build.

Cost and schedule performance of major public projects is the direct test of a state turning plans into functioning systems, and rich countries often do it badly. It should be the priority data build for this dimension.
Young firms that scale show organisations being built, but the rate is an outcome of markets, finance and regulation together. Coverage outside OECD members is missing.

An economic structure share that reads development stage and comparative advantage, not the capacity to turn plans into systems. National accounts undercount informal manufacturing, though income bias is low and non-monotonic.
Reads position in global assembly chains rather than design or build capability, and only formal exports. A weak proxy.
Freight forwarders' perception of an infrastructure stock that money buys. Retirement is right.
Small-scale delivery outcome measured for a hypothetical formal business. Retired and superseded.

End-to-end delivery is an outcome of build capacity, but supply reliability is a stock that money buys, and it observes only formal firms connecting to formal grids; off-grid and community solar building is invisible. Covers 82 of 135 countries.
Breadth of what a country can make competitively is a reasonable outcome of accumulated build capability, but it correlates strongly with income and sees only formal exports.

Overrun on cost and schedule is a direct read of execution that rich countries can fail on, so it should be weakly income-linked. It reads state megaprojects only and misses distributed building such as self-built housing and community infrastructure. No data.
Growth of young firms is an outcome of building organisations, but registry-based business dynamics data count only formal firms and miss informal enterprises that grow. Coverage is OECD-only.
A sector share that follows development stage and resource endowment, and it peaks in middle-income states then falls. It rewards industrial structure rather than delivering systems.
Assembly hubs score high without owning design, so it reads where a global value chain sits. Its link to income is non-monotonic, but it is still more about trade position than state delivery.
A freight forwarder perception of infrastructure, income-linked and small-country biased. Retirement is correct.
Days to connect is a measured delivery result for a small system, but the series is frozen at 2019 and was expert-reported. Retired and replaced.

End-to-end delivery of connections is the best observable building signal here, and it is an outcome. It folds in supply reliability, which depends on grid investment, and B-READY covers 82 of 135 countries.
Complexity measures are known to track income very closely, so it mostly restates how rich and industrial a country is. It reads export sophistication, not the ability to deliver systems.

Cost and schedule performance on real projects is the direct test of converting plans into working systems, and overruns happen in rich countries too. No dataset yet, and project mix and reporting differ.
Young firms reaching scale is an outcome of finance and market size as much as building capability. Coverage is irregular and absent for large emerging economies. No data.
The WGI reads the democratic channel through perception, which is adjacent to collective purpose and tied to income. Retirement is right.
Tax collection shows a society funding a common project through the state, and it reads fiscal capacity, a core institution. Federal structure, resource rents and income level all distort it.

The Gini is a structural condition that may constrain a common project, so it is an input at best, not an outcome of shared purpose. It reads distribution, which institutions shape, but it is not the construct.
Belonging is close to the construct, but any attitudinal item risks reading nationalism or deference. Leaving it a gap until an item passes the regime test is right.
Giving time to an organisation is a behaviour of acting for a common project through durable organisations. It is self-reported and the Gallup source is not inspectable.
Hostile polarisation constrains collective action, but the V-Dem item reads calm under repression as pluralism. Keeping it as a check is right until a measure can separate the two.

Membership of charitable organisations reads the organisational fabric through which people act for strangers, which is an institutional channel for shared purpose. Membership is not activity and the question format differs between EVS and WVS.
Reads the democratic channel as perceived by experts, not whether people see themselves in a common project. Retirement is right.

Tax capacity rises with formalisation and income, and in informal economies people fund public goods through community levies, remittances and mutual aid that never appear. Federal and resource confounds add noise.
A structural condition on seeing a common project, not a measure of it, so I refile it as I. Regional patterns (Latin America, Southern Africa) dominate its variation.
Belonging is adjacent to the construct, but any attitudinal item risks reading regime deference. Leaving it unfilled until a regime-neutral item exists is right.

Giving time to others is an observed act of common purpose, and Gallup-type data show high rates in poorer countries such as Indonesia and Kenya. A definition limited to organisations would still miss informal helping, so it should include that.
Expert-coded and unable to tell pluralist calm from suppressed calm. Keeping it as an unscored check is right.

Reported membership is a behaviour near acting for strangers, but membership in formal organisations misses informal mutual-aid groups, savings circles and religious charity that carry collective action in LMICs. Question format inflates the spread.
It measures the democratic channel and not seeing oneself in a common project, which the Singapore case shows. A perception composite correlated with income. Retirement is correct.
Tax take rises with income and formal economy size, and is confounded by federal structure and resource rents. It poorly signals willingness to fund common goods.

It is a structural condition and not a measure of shared purpose, and a value judgement enters through it. Inequality has a loose link to income; survey gaps and consumption-based Ginis hamper comparison.
Belonging is the target construct, if an item reads the same across regimes. It is a self-report with regime-type bias, and no series exists.
Volunteering is observed behaviour for a common cause, with moderate income link. Reported by survey and not by records, so O and not C; proprietary microdata means no data.
Hostile division matters to a common project, but expert coding reads calm in regimes with no opposition, and the target is pluralism. No scored data, and wealth has little to do with it.

Membership in charitable organisations is self-reported behaviour toward strangers, so O and not C. It is closer to the construct than outcomes like tax, but question format varies and membership is not activity; wealthier countries do read higher.

Article volume is a research-system output that feeds sensing, so it reads better as an input to anticipation than as an outcome of it; it says nothing about whether any institution uses the knowledge to prepare for change. Its cross-country variation follows income per head and university funding closely.

A national statistical system is a durable institution that outlasts its staff, and its ability to measure the country is a precondition for anticipation that can be observed and compared. It measures sensing of the present, not preparation for the future, and richer states score higher, but several middle-income systems outperform their income.

A mandated foresight function with continuity across governments is the closest direct institutional measure of this dimension. The score should weight statutory mandate, budget line and survival across changes of government over existence alone, because a unit that exists only on paper or depends on one minister is not capability; with no data the construct is strong but unproven.

A public funder that awards grants of five years or more shows an institution willing to bind itself to a horizon, which is a real anticipation behaviour, better than a spending-mix share. It reads research-funding governance rather than whole-of-government preparation, and the grant-duration rules of a few large funders can drive the national figure; with no data, uncertainty is wide.

Article volume is an output of a funded, formal research system and tracks income per head closely. It says little about whether a society notices and prepares for change. It also misses applied, local-language and practitioner knowledge, which is where much sensing happens in large low- and middle-income countries.

A working statistical system is a precondition for official sensing, so it is an input, not a direct measure of anticipation. It scores only what the state records formally and can read low where informal economies and community monitoring carry the signal. Several middle-income countries score well, so the income link is real but not total.

Existence, mandate and continuity of a foresight unit describe an institutional arrangement, which is an input; a C filing needs evidence that the unit changes decisions. It is top-down by design and ignores distributed anticipation by firms, civil society and communities, so any index Envisioning builds should score use, not existence.

A five-year grant is an observable decision to wait for a result, so C is a fair filing, but it measures patience in formal public research funding, which is adjacent to anticipation rather than central to it. Grant registers exist mostly where funders are rich and digitised, so coverage gaps will correlate with income; the redundancy with articles is partial, through the shared research-system base.
Article volume per head tracks research funding and university density, which scale with income. It records past research output, not the ability to spot emerging change.
The SPI measures data-system quality, an input to sensing. Statistical offices are largely funded by national income, so rich countries lead; it shows capacity to see, not any act of anticipating.
A mandated, continuous foresight function is a direct and cheap institutional choice that poorer states can make, so it is low in income proxy. No data exists, so it carries no score until built.

Grant duration shows a funder choosing to wait, which is behaviour rather than budget size, and the share form removes most scale. Still unwired, and only countries with large grant systems have registers; the link to anticipating change is indirect.

Patent filings record attempts that a working IP office and enforceable property rights made worth registering, so the count reads institutional legal infrastructure as much as experimentation. Strategic and subsidised filing (Korea, China, US) and income distort it, and patents are costly, so they miss cheap attempts.

Trademarks are cheap and frequent, so they track many small market attempts better than patents. They also count rebranding and defensive filings, and the count depends on how accessible the national registry is.

It mostly duplicates trademark counts and carries subsidy (China) and filing-route (EUIPO, Benelux) artefacts that are institutional quirks rather than experimentation. Its marginal information over trademarks is low.

New repositories count cheap individual attempts, but they rest on individual effort on a foreign private platform, not on any national institution that lets attempts be tested, ended or scaled. Coursework, hub effects and access gates add noise, and connectivity and developer density follow income.

First rounds count attempts that outside risk capital chose to back, which needs working contract law, exit routes and investor protection, so it is a downstream outcome of the institutional environment rather than a direct capability measure; refiled from C to O. Venture markets concentrate in rich countries, and with no inspectable source uncertainty is wide.

TEA counts people starting businesses, and in low-income economies much of that is necessity self-employment that compensates for weak labour markets and institutions, which is not capability; refiled from C to O. The negative income relation inverts the wealth proxy rather than removing it.

An attitude survey of individuals does not show whether institutions let failure end cheaply. It is a weak perception proxy and the denominator does not match the label; insolvency efficiency now measures the institutional substitute.

The time and cost of a court-run exit measure directly whether the legal system lets an attempt be abandoned and its assets reused, which is the institutional core of experimentation. Richer countries have better courts, but the B-READY score varies across income bands; the zero-when-unused rule and 82 of 135 coverage limit it.

Firms admitted to and exiting a regulator's controlled trial regime is the most direct measure of a state institution letting new approaches be tested under rules and then ended or authorised. Counts per head favour small financial hubs, and regulator definitions differ, so a built register needs one definition before scores mean anything.

Spinouts are an outcome of university technology-transfer institutions and IP rules, so they read a real institutional route from research to attempt, but they are downstream and refiled from C to O. Incompatible national definitions and their dependence on research spending make them a weak comparable measure.

Retirement is correct: the share of R&D that business performs describes the composition of a spending stock and the ownership model, not how easily attempts start and stop. It confounds large business research with a tiny research base dominated by one firm.

Patents count only experiments that reached a costly formal filing, so they undercount the cheap, informal and frugal attempts typical of large low- and middle-income economies. Strategic and subsidised filing in Korea, the US and China further separates the count from attempts.

Trademarks are cheaper and closer to many small market attempts than patents, so validity is better. They still count only firms that formalised, and miss informal traders who try new products without registering anything.
Designs share the formal-registration bias of trademarks, and the EUIPO, Benelux and Chinese subsidy distortions add noise that is not capability. It adds little that trademarks do not already carry.

This is the closest indicator in the set to cheap, unregistered, distributed attempts: no fee, no lawyer, abandonment kept on record. It is still gated by connectivity, one platform and English-language developer culture, and coursework inflates it, so it reads a digital slice of experimentation rather than the whole.

A count of first rounds is better than an amount, but it records attempts only after outside risk money arrives, so it is an outcome of experimentation and of capital depth, not a direct capability measure. It ignores the family, rotating savings and informal finance that fund most first attempts in low- and middle-income countries.

A household survey counts people trying, including informal and unregistered businesses, so it is the best available direct measure of how many attempts a population makes. Necessity entrepreneurship inflates it, but from this stance that is still attempting, and the income gradient runs partly the other way, so wealth proxy risk is low.

Stated fear of failure is attitudinal and culturally inflected, so P is right. It does reach people outside the formal sector, which the court-based insolvency measure cannot, so it complements rather than duplicates insolvency efficiency.

It measures the cost of a formal court exit, which matters only for firms that formalised; most failed attempts in large low- and middle-income countries close informally and never reach a court. Score 0 for an unused formal exit can mean informal exit works, not that failure is costly, so validity as a measure of abandoning attempts is low.

Counting firms through sandboxes is a direct observation of a state letting attempts happen under relaxed rules, so C fits. It covers only regulated, mostly fintech, firms and favours countries with well-resourced regulators, while informal markets experiment without asking permission.

Spinouts are an outcome of a funded university research and tech-transfer system, not a direct capability measure, and the C filing should be corrected. They are a narrow, elite channel of experimentation and track income per head and research spending closely.

The retirement is correct: it reads the structure of a formal spending stock and ownership model, not whether new approaches are tried. It is blind to the informal and frugal experimentation that never enters R&D accounts.
Patent filing tracks R&D spend and legal capacity per head and is distorted by subsidy and strategy filings. It counts completed filings, not how easily attempts are made or dropped.
Trademarks are cheap and frequent, but mix branding, retail and service activity that follows market size and income. Small-country and fee-structure effects add noise.
Design filings partly duplicate trademarks, are subsidy-inflated in China, and miss EU and Benelux filings made at regional offices. The measure is biased by filing geography, not capability.

Nearly free attempts are a good fit for the dimension, but access to computers, connectivity and a developer workforce scales with income. Platform coverage and location errors, and the access gate for China, limit it.

A count of first rounds reflects attempts that outside investors funded, which depends on deep capital markets and wealth. It is an outcome of financial depth more than a direct capability, and no data exists.

TEA counts people trying, and necessity entrepreneurship in poorer countries pushes it up, so it is not a rich-country measure and partly runs against income. It is a survey outcome of attempts, not the ease of attempting; value of attempts is unseen.
A self-reported attitude among those who already see opportunity, so it is cultural and perception-based. The link to wealth is mixed, but it says nothing about the real cost of failing.

Time and cost of formal exit is an observable rule-in-use that governs abandoning an attempt. It correlates with income through court capacity, and zero scores can mean no use of the procedure rather than a bad one.

Firms passing through sandboxes show a state actively permitting trials, a decision rather than a purchase. Poorer states with fintech regimes can score well. No data exists and definitions vary across regulators.

Spinouts depend on research university size, technology transfer offices and funding, which follow income. Definitions are incompatible and no data exists; it is an outcome of research systems rather than easy experimentation.
The business share reads the make-up of a spending stock and the ownership model, not the ease of trying new things. It is disqualified and unscored, and retiring it is correct.
